MARANA, Arizona (CNN) — I have been privileged in the past to watch Tiger Woods on a golf course. And I can tell you, it can be a painful and frustrating experience.

Golf fans flocked to Arizona to witness Tiger make his long-awaited return to the tee. Not because the golf he produces is anything less than spectacular—and, at times, utterly dazzling—but because the sheer volume of people he attracts convinces me, time and again, that golf must be one of the most challenging spectator sports to watch “out on the course.” That is just my opinion, though.

Try telling that to the legions who made their way to Arizona this week once they heard the world’s top player was returning to the game after more than eight months away. Woods’ first competitive taste of action in the better part of a year was not due to get under way until around lunchtime here, but judging by the number of fans already out on the course, you would have thought his tee time was closer to 7 a.m.

Even those jostling for position to catch a glimpse of him on the range or the putting green were taking no chances, making sure they arrived in plenty of time. Remember, all of this was before he had even teed off.

The scene on the first hole was, as expected, bustling to say the least. The small gantries were already packed because of the impressive array of talent on show throughout the week, but the atmosphere grew even more frenzied when the Woods-Jones match-up was announced. Mayhem, to say the least.

Those seated in the stands were the lucky ones. I felt for the unfortunate spectators forced to stand and strain every sinew just to catch a glimpse of that first shot from the world number one. Even we in the media suffered. With only seconds to go before the American struck his drive, one television camera crew—which really should have known better—blatantly blocked us from getting that prized shot. Only some quick, last-gasp thinking from our cameraman, John, saved the day.

In case you were wondering, that Woods drive was majestic, and he went on to win the first two holes in fine style. When he strode off down the first fairway, a stampede followed, as spectators braved the soaring Arizona temperatures to follow him every step of the way.

The Woods “wow factor” is still very much alive and kicking. The question is whether the so-called bionic knee will hold up in the weeks and months to come.

MARANA, Arizona (CNN) -- I’ve had the good fortune before to watch Tiger Woods play golf in person. I can also say that doing so can be an uncomfortable and exasperating experience.

Golf supporters poured into Arizona to witness Tiger’s much-anticipated return to the tee. That was not because his golf is anything less than exceptional — at times it is absolutely brilliant — but because the enormous crowds he draws always remind me why golf may be one of the worst sports to watch while walking the course. That is only my view, of course.

Still, try saying that to the thousands who made their way to Arizona this week after learning that the world’s number one player was coming back to competition following an absence of more than eight months.

Woods was not scheduled to begin his first competitive appearance in nearly a year until around midday local time. But judging from the number of spectators already spread across the course, you could easily have believed he was due to tee off at 7 a.m. Fans trying to secure a spot to see him on the practice range or putting green were not taking any risks; they made sure they arrived well ahead of time. And all of this happened before he had even hit his opening tee shot.

The atmosphere at the first hole was, predictably, extremely busy. The small grandstands were already full because of the impressive group of players competing during the week, but the excitement intensified even further once the Woods-Jones pairing was announced. It was chaos, to put it mildly.

The people with seats in the stands were the fortunate ones. I felt sorry for those standing, stretching and straining just to get a view of the world number one’s first shot. Even the media had difficulties. Moments before the American hit his drive, a television camera crew — who really should have been more aware — plainly blocked our view of the key shot. Only some quick, last-second action from our cameraman John rescued the situation.

In case you are curious, Woods’ drive was magnificent, and he went on to take the first two holes in impressive fashion.

As he marched away down the opening fairway, a rush of spectators followed, determined to endure the intense Arizona heat and track him at every stage. The “wow factor” surrounding Woods clearly remains as strong as ever.

The remaining question is whether his so-called bionic knee will withstand the demands of the coming weeks and months.

**MARANA, Arizona (CNN) —** Tiger Woods returned to competitive golf Wednesday after an eight-month absence, and the scene at the first tee made clear that the sport had been waiting for him.

Long before Woods arrived, fans packed the ropes several deep at the Ritz-Carlton Golf Club at Dove Mountain, craning for a glimpse of the world No. 1 as he made his comeback from reconstructive knee surgery. Television crews, photographers and reporters swarmed the practice area and tee box, turning an early-round match into a major-championship-style spectacle.

When Woods finally stepped onto the first tee, the noise surged. Cameras clicked in waves. Spectators lifted phones and leaned over shoulders for a view. Then came the moment everyone had come to see: Woods settled over the ball and sent his opening tee shot into the Arizona desert air, a controlled swing that drew an immediate roar from the gallery.

The shot mattered, but so did the motion. Every step, pivot and follow-through was being studied for signs of how his surgically repaired left knee would hold up under tournament pressure. Woods has not played competitively since winning the U.S. Open in dramatic fashion last June, when he defeated Rocco Mediate in a playoff while later revealing he had been competing with a torn ACL and stress fractures.

His return here at the WGC-Accenture Match Play Championship is about more than one result. It is the first real test of whether golf’s biggest star can again withstand the strain of walking 18 holes, swinging at full speed and grinding through pressure situations.

Woods appeared composed, acknowledging the crowd but keeping his focus narrow. Still, the atmosphere around him was anything but routine. Security tried to keep pathways clear as media members jockeyed for position, and spectators rushed from hole to hole to follow his match.

For the PGA Tour, his return brings back its central attraction. For Woods, it begins the next phase of a comeback that will be measured not only in birdies and victories, but in the durability of a rebuilt knee that has become one of the biggest questions in sports.

On Wednesday in Marana, the answer began with one tee shot — and with thousands watching every inch of it.

**Following Tiger Woods in Arizona Is Almost Impossible — and That Says Everything About His Comeback**

SCOTTSDALE, Ariz. — I knew Tiger Woods’ return would draw a crowd. I did not expect it to feel like trying to follow a parade through a sold-out stadium.

From the moment Woods stepped onto the course in Arizona, the atmosphere around him was less like a golf tournament and more like a major sporting event compressed into a few narrow ropes and cart paths. Spectators surged toward every tee box, fairway landing area and green, all hoping for a glimpse of the most famous golfer of his generation making another comeback.

Seeing him, though, was the hard part.

I tried to follow Woods from hole to hole, but the enormous turnout made it nearly impossible to get a clear view. Fans were stacked five, six, sometimes even more rows deep along the ropes. People stood on tiptoes, held phones above their heads and leaned around shoulders just to catch a flash of his swing. At times, the only way to know where Woods was came from the movement of the crowd itself — a roar rising in the distance, then a wave of spectators rushing toward the next shot.

On several holes, I saw little more than his cap moving between caddies, security and television crews. When he reached the green, the gallery tightened again, hundreds of people pressing forward as marshals pleaded for space. Every practice swing drew attention. Every step was followed. Every putt, whether routine or meaningful, felt like a shared event.

The Arizona setting only amplified the spectacle. Bright sun, packed grandstands and the familiar desert backdrop gave the day a festival feel, but Woods’ presence changed the rhythm of the tournament. Other groups moved through with relative calm. Around Woods, there was constant motion — spectators jogging ahead, craning for position, asking strangers what club he hit or whether anyone had actually seen the ball land.

For many fans, the score seemed almost secondary. They came to witness the comeback, to say they had been there when Woods returned again to competitive golf. Some spoke about his past victories. Others talked about his injuries and the uncertainty that has surrounded each attempt to resume his career. Parents lifted children onto their shoulders. Longtime fans wore red shirts, even though it was not Sunday. Phones stayed ready.

As a reporter, it was frustrating. As a scene, it was remarkable.

Woods has spent years turning ordinary tournament rounds into events, and even now, with questions about his health and form, the pull remains unmistakable. The size of the crowd made it difficult to watch the golf in any traditional sense, but it also revealed the scale of his presence. Few athletes can make a Thursday or Friday round feel this crowded, this urgent, this loud.

By the time Woods moved deeper into the course, I had accepted that following him shot-for-shot was a losing battle. The better view was not always of the swing itself, but of the reaction around it: the sudden hush before impact, the burst of sound after contact, the scramble of thousands trying to keep up.

Tiger Woods’ comeback in Arizona was hard to see. But it was impossible to miss.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a 2009-era CNN golf feature on Tiger Woods’ return at the WGC Match Play in Marana, including the fans arriving early, the packed first hole, his match with Jones, and his “bionic knee.”
counterfactuals.output:
**MARANA, Arizona (CNN) —** The desert was still cool and the sun only beginning to climb over the mountains when the first wave of fans started pouring through the gates at the Ritz-Carlton Golf Club.

They had come early — very early — for one reason.

Tiger Woods was back.

Eight months after limping to one of the most dramatic victories in golf history at the U.S. Open, then disappearing from competition to rebuild his left knee, Woods returned Wednesday at the WGC-Accenture Match Play Championship. And even before he struck a shot that counted, the scene made clear that the sport had been waiting with him.

By the time Woods arrived at the first tee for his opening-round match against Australia’s Brendan Jones, the gallery around the hole was several rows deep. Fans leaned over ropes, held cameras high and craned for a glimpse of the world No. 1. Some had raced straight to the first tee after the gates opened, staking out positions as if for a Sunday back nine rather than a Wednesday morning start.

Woods, dressed in black pants and a light shirt, walked with little visible hesitation. The left knee — surgically reconstructed after his epic playoff win over Rocco Mediate at Torrey Pines — was the day’s co-star. Every stride, every shift of weight, every full-blooded swing was watched for clues.

If Woods felt the attention, he did not show it for long.

After months of rehabilitation, speculation and carefully managed practice reports, Woods’ first competitive hole was greeted like a major championship moment. The applause swelled as he was introduced, then fell into silence as he settled over the ball. His opening tee shot was less about perfection than confirmation: Tiger Woods was again inside the ropes.

Jones, ranked well below Woods but hardly anonymous in the match-play format, faced the strangest assignment in golf — not only trying to beat Woods, but trying to do it on the day the game’s biggest star returned from injury. Match play can reduce reputations quickly; one bad hole is only one lost hole. But against Woods, the pressure rarely feels so contained.

The question entering the week was not just whether Woods could win. It was whether the knee would hold up under competitive strain: walking 18 holes, hitting from uneven desert lies, rotating violently through the ball, and doing it all with the intensity that had defined his career.

Woods had joked before the tournament about his rebuilt joint, calling it a kind of “bionic knee.” The phrase fit the mood. After major surgery, months away from the PGA Tour and a rehabilitation process conducted mostly out of public view, his return carried a hint of science fiction: the champion rebuilt, reassembled and released back into competition.

But the golf course offered more ordinary tests. Could he find fairways? Could he control distance? Could he summon touch around firm greens? Could he handle the fatigue that comes not from the gym, but from playing when every shot matters?

Early on, the answer appeared encouraging. Woods’ swing looked powerful, his balance largely sound. There were moments of rust, as expected, but also flashes of the familiar rhythm — the focused walk, the clipped club twirl, the quick stare after impact that told the gallery he already knew where the ball was headed.

For the fans pressed around the first tee and lining the fairways in Marana, that was enough. They had not come merely to watch a first-round match. They had come to witness a return.

Golf had continued in Woods’ absence, but it had felt different. Television ratings dipped, tournament energy shifted, and every major storyline seemed to include the same missing presence. His comeback in the Arizona desert did not guarantee immediate dominance, and match play is an unforgiving place to test a repaired body and a dormant competitive game.

Still, on this morning, the scoreboard felt secondary.

Tiger Woods was walking again. Tiger Woods was swinging again. And judging by the packed ropes at the first hole, golf’s biggest attraction had lost none of his pull.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
The first sign that Tiger Woods was back was not the swing. It was the sound.

Long before he appeared on the tee, the low murmur around the opening hole had turned into a rolling, restless buzz, the kind that moves through a crowd before a concert headliner steps out from behind the curtain. Fans stood five and six deep along the ropes, phones raised, necks craned, children perched on shoulders. Tournament volunteers kept reminding spectators to keep the pathways clear, but there was no disguising the pull of the moment: after a long injury absence, Woods was about to hit a competitive tee shot again.

The media scrum was nearly as crowded as the gallery. Reporters, photographers and camera operators jostled for sightlines, only to find the prime angles swallowed by television crews and their towering equipment. Boom mics hovered. Handheld cameras edged forward. A moving wall of broadcast staff seemed to seal off the view at precisely the wrong moments, leaving print reporters and still photographers leaning, ducking and muttering as they tried to catch even a glimpse of Woods’ final rehearsal swings.

Then the crowd quieted.

Woods stepped onto the tee with the familiar red-and-black aura replaced by the more practical tension of a man testing a repaired body under the full weight of expectation. He moved deliberately, not hurried, acknowledging the reception with a brief nod. The applause swelled, then broke into cheers, then settled again into silence as he bent to place the ball on the tee.

For a few seconds, the entire property seemed to hold its breath.

His swing, when it came, was unmistakably his — compact, balanced, controlled, with that sudden violent acceleration through the ball that made the years fall away. The strike cracked through the cool air, sharp and pure. Heads snapped down the fairway. The ball climbed on a strong, majestic line, turning gently before settling safely in the short grass.

For an instant, nobody moved. Then the place erupted.

The cheer began at the tee and rolled outward, chased by applause from fans farther down the hole who had seen the ball finish. Woods bent to pick up his tee, expression unreadable but composed, and began walking. That was the cue.

What followed was less a gallery movement than a stampede.

Thousands surged down the fairway ropes in a wave, marshals backpedaling, photographers jogging with long lenses bouncing against their hips, TV crews hustling to stay ahead of him. Fans who had waited hours for one swing now sprint-walked to the next vantage point, kicking up dust and crushed grass, calling to friends, holding phones aloft to record the march.

Woods did not break stride. He walked in the middle of it all — surrounded, scrutinized, celebrated — as if reentering a world that had been waiting for him to return. The drive had been only one shot, the first swing in a long day and perhaps a longer comeback. But in that moment, with the crowd pouring after him down the fairway, it felt like something larger: not merely a tee shot, but a reawakening.

**In Arizona, Tiger Woods Returns — and So Does the Roar, Even If the View Is Awful**

*SCOTTSDALE, Ariz.* — By midmorning, the desert sun had already begun pressing down on the gallery, bouncing off cart paths and bleached grandstands, turning the long walk between holes into something closer to a test of endurance than a day at the golf course. Spectators craned their necks three-deep behind ropes. Volunteers barked for movement where there was nowhere to move. Cell phones rose like periscopes from a sea of hats, most people seeing little more than a red shirt, a familiar gait, and the backs of strangers’ heads.

And still, when Tiger Woods appeared, the place changed.

That remains the strangest and most durable fact about Woods in this late chapter of his career: even when the logistics are maddening, even when the sightlines are poor, even when the promise of seeing him play golf becomes, in practice, an afternoon of shuffling, waiting, guessing and watching reactions ripple through the crowd before the ball is ever visible — he can still make a golf tournament feel like an event.

Arizona had been waiting for him. Golf had been waiting for him. Perhaps Woods himself had been waiting, too, for a version of competitive life that could still accommodate the battered right leg, the rebuilt body, the reduced schedule and the impossibly high standard he created in another athletic lifetime.

His comeback was not the return of the old Tiger, because that golfer no longer exists. The violence of the swing has been tempered. The walk between shots is more deliberate. Every slope looks like a negotiation. There are moments, especially on longer transitions, when the physical cost is plain enough that the crowd quiets not out of etiquette, but concern.

Then he pulls a club, sets his feet, turns through the ball — and the old electricity snaps back on.

A piercing iron into a tucked pin. A recovery shot from desert trouble that seems to travel through a window no one else could see. A putt that begins outside the cup, curls obediently, and drops to a roar that rolls across the property. These are not merely good shots. Plenty of good shots are struck at professional golf tournaments. These are Tiger shots, and the distinction is still understood instantly by anyone within earshot.

That is his “wow factor,” stubbornly alive after all these years. It survives the surgeries, the scandals, the layoffs, the comebacks to the comebacks. It survives even the modern spectator experience, which at times seems almost designed to frustrate the very people who paid to witness it.

For many fans following Woods in Arizona, the day was less a viewing experience than a pilgrimage. They walked, waited, sweated and hoped. They caught fragments: the top of his cap, the finish of a swing, a ball landing somewhere beyond a human wall. On certain holes, unless one had arrived early enough to stake out territory, there was no realistic chance of seeing both the shot and its result. Movement around the course became a slow squeeze through bottlenecks, with marshals pleading for order and fans wondering why a sport so dependent on atmosphere can still be so indifferent to basic crowd flow.

The complaints were legitimate. The affection was undeniable.

“Did you see it?” one man asked after Woods sent an approach toward the flag.

“No,” his friend said, smiling anyway. “But I heard it.”

That, in miniature, was the day.

Woods’ score mattered, of course, because scoreboards are the sport’s final editors. Yet it did not fully define the occasion. With Woods now, every round is measured on two ledgers. There is the competitive ledger — fairways hit, putts converted, ground gained or lost. And there is the human ledger: how he moved, how he recovered, whether he could summon enough brilliance to remind everyone why they had come.

On that second count, the answer was emphatic.

He is no longer inevitable. He may never again be the weekly menace who made Sunday afternoons feel preordained. But inevitability has been replaced by something more fragile and, in its way, more compelling: possibility. Every time Woods tees it up now, there is the chance that the body will object, that rust will show, that the younger generation will make the distance between eras look as wide as the desert horizon.

There is also the chance that he will do something no one else in the field can make feel quite the same.

That is why they came in Arizona. Not for comfort. Certainly not for convenience. They came because Tiger Woods remains one of the few athletes whose presence can turn a routine tournament moment into a shared jolt of disbelief.

The galleries grumbled, shuffled and strained to see. Then Woods hit a shot, and they roared as if they had witnessed all of it.

In truth, some had. Most had not. But with Tiger, even now, sometimes the sound is enough.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
